prompt: In valence bond terms, how are the two carbons of a C=C double bond hybridized?

choices.text: Both are sp2
Both are sp3
choices.why: sp3 carbons form four single bonds. Double-bond carbons are sp2, with one unhybridized p orbital left for the π bond.

choices.text: Both are sp
choices.why: The carbons of a double bond have three hybrid orbitals at 120° to one another, which is sp2.

choices.text: One is sp2 and one is sp3
choices.why: Both carbons are sp2; each contributes a p orbital to the π bond.

explanation: The carbons of a double bond are sp2-hybridized, with three equivalent hybrid orbitals in a plane at 120° to one another. They form a σ bond by head-on overlap of sp2 orbitals and a π bond by sideways overlap of unhybridized p orbitals.

prompt: At what angle do the three sp2 hybrid orbitals of a double-bond carbon lie to one another, in degrees?
explanation: The three equivalent sp2 hybrid orbitals lie in a plane at angles of 120° to one another. The unhybridized p orbital is perpendicular to that plane.

prompt: How is the π bond of a carbon–carbon double bond formed?

choices.text: By sideways overlap of unhybridized p orbitals
By head-on overlap of sp2 hybrid orbitals
choices.why: Head-on overlap of sp2 orbitals forms the σ bond of the double bond.

choices.text: By sideways overlap of sp2 hybrid orbitals
choices.why: The sp2 orbitals lie in the plane and form σ bonds. The π bond uses the leftover p orbitals.

choices.text: By head-on overlap of unhybridized p orbitals
choices.why: The two p orbitals are parallel and overlap sideways, not head-on.

explanation: The carbons form a σ bond by head-on overlap of sp2 orbitals and a π bond by sideways overlap of unhybridized p orbitals oriented perpendicular to the sp2 plane.

prompt: In molecular orbital terms, which π molecular orbital of a C=C bond has a node between the nuclei?

choices.text: The antibonding π MO, formed by combining p lobes of different algebraic signs
The bonding π MO, formed by combining p lobes of the same algebraic sign
choices.why: The bonding π MO has no node between the nuclei.

choices.text: The bonding π MO, formed by combining p lobes of different algebraic signs
choices.why: Lobes of different signs give the antibonding MO, and the bonding MO has no node between the nuclei.

choices.text: The antibonding π MO, formed by combining p lobes of the same algebraic sign
choices.why: Lobes of the same sign give the bonding MO. The antibonding MO comes from lobes of different signs.

explanation: Interaction between the two p orbitals gives one bonding and one antibonding π MO. The bonding MO has no node between nuclei and comes from lobes with the same algebraic sign; the antibonding MO has a node between nuclei and comes from lobes with different signs.

prompt: Why is the barrier to rotation around a C=C double bond at least as large as the strength of the π bond?

choices.text: For rotation to occur, the π bond must break and then re-form
For rotation to occur, the σ bond must break
choices.why: The σ bond's head-on overlap isn't affected by rotation. Twisting the p orbitals out of alignment breaks the π bond.

choices.text: The substituents on the two carbons collide during rotation
choices.why: The barrier comes from breaking the π bond, not from crowding of substituents.

choices.text: The carbons must first rehybridize from sp2 to sp
choices.why: No rehybridization is involved. Twisting the p orbitals until they are perpendicular breaks the π bond.

explanation: Rotating one end of a double bond turns the p orbitals out of alignment until they are perpendicular, so the π bond must break and re-form (Figure 7.4.1). The barrier must therefore be at least as great as the π bond strength, an estimated 350 kJ/mol, compared with only 12 kJ/mol for rotation in ethane.

prompt: What is the estimated strength of the π bond, and so the minimum barrier to rotation around a C=C double bond, in kJ/mol?
explanation: The barrier to double-bond rotation must be at least as great as the π bond strength, an estimated 350 kJ/mol (84 kcal/mol). By contrast, the barrier to bond rotation in ethane is only 12 kJ/mol.

prompt: What does it mean to call an alkene disubstituted?

choices.text: Two groups other than hydrogen are attached to the double-bond carbons
Its carbon chain contains two separate double bonds
choices.why: A compound with two double bonds is a diene. Disubstituted refers to the groups on the double-bond carbons.

choices.text: Each of its double-bond carbons carries two hydrogen atoms
choices.why: That describes ethylene, which has no substituents other than hydrogen.

choices.text: Two of its hydrogens have been replaced by halogen atoms
choices.why: Disubstituted counts any two non-hydrogen groups on the double-bond carbons, such as the two methyls of 2-butene.

explanation: Disubstituted means that two substituents other than hydrogen are bonded to the double-bond carbons. 2-Butene, CH3CH=CHCH3, is an example: each double-bond carbon carries one methyl group.

prompt: How are the methyl groups arranged in cis-2-butene?

choices.text: On the same side of the double bond
On opposite sides of the double bond
choices.why: That is trans-2-butene.

choices.text: Both on the same double-bond carbon
choices.why: That would be 2-methylpropene, (CH3)2C=CH2. In 2-butene each double-bond carbon has one methyl.

choices.text: Perpendicular to the plane of the double bond
choices.why: Groups on sp2 carbons lie in the plane of the double bond. Cis and trans describe same side versus opposite sides.

explanation: The two methyl groups in 2-butene can be on the same side or on opposite sides of the double bond. The isomer with substituents on the same side is cis-2-butene; the one with substituents on opposite sides is trans-2-butene (Figure 7.4.2).

prompt: Why are cis-2-butene and trans-2-butene different compounds that can be isolated separately?

choices.text: Rotation around the double bond can't occur, so they can't interconvert
They have different molecular formulas, so they are different compounds
choices.why: Both are C4H8. They differ only in the arrangement of the methyl groups around the double bond.

choices.text: Their double bonds are in different positions in the chain
choices.why: In both, the double bond is between C2 and C3. They differ in geometry, not in where the double bond is.

choices.text: Their carbon atoms are connected to one another in a different order
choices.why: The atoms are connected in the same order; only their arrangement on either side of the double bond differs.

explanation: Since bond rotation can't occur, the two 2-butenes can't spontaneously interconvert; they are different, isolable compounds. As with disubstituted cycloalkanes, they are called cis–trans stereoisomers.

prompt: When is cis–trans isomerism possible in an alkene?

choices.text: When each double-bond carbon is attached to two different groups
Whenever the alkene is disubstituted
choices.why: Not every disubstituted alkene qualifies: in (CH3)2C=CH2 one carbon carries two identical groups. And the rule isn't limited to disubstituted alkenes.

choices.text: When at least one double-bond carbon is attached to two different groups
choices.why: Both carbons must carry two different groups. If either carbon has two identical groups, cis–trans isomerism isn't possible.

choices.text: Only when the double bond is part of a ring
choices.why: Open-chain alkenes such as 2-butene have cis and trans isomers.

explanation: Cis–trans isomerism can occur whenever both double-bond carbons are attached to two different groups. If one of the double-bond carbons is attached to two identical groups, cis–trans isomerism is not possible (Figure 7.4.3).

prompt: Which of these compounds can exist as a pair of cis–trans isomers?

choices.text: CH3CH2CH=CHCH3
CH3CH=CH2
choices.why: The CH2 carbon carries two identical groups (two hydrogens), so no cis–trans isomers exist.

choices.text: (CH3)2C=CHCH3
choices.why: One double-bond carbon carries two identical methyl groups, so cis–trans isomerism isn't possible.

choices.text: (CH3)2C=C(CH3)CH2CH3
choices.why: One double-bond carbon carries two identical methyl groups, so cis–trans isomerism isn't possible.

explanation: In CH3CH2CH=CHCH3, one double-bond carbon carries H and CH3 and the other carries H and CH2CH3. Both carbons have two different groups, so cis and trans isomers exist.

prompt: How many of these five compounds can exist as cis–trans isomers: CH3CH=CH2, (CH3)2C=CHCH3, CH3CH2CH=CHCH3, (CH3)2C=C(CH3)CH2CH3, ClCH=CHCl?
explanation: Only CH3CH2CH=CHCH3 and ClCH=CHCl have two different groups on each double-bond carbon. CH3CH=CH2 has two hydrogens on one carbon, and both (CH3)2C= compounds have two identical methyls on one carbon.

prompt: The housefly sex attractant cis-9-tricosene is an unbranched alkene with 23 carbons and one double bond. Tricosane, the straight-chain alkane, is C23H48. How many hydrogens does cis-9-tricosene have?
explanation: One double bond means two fewer hydrogens than the alkane, so cis-9-tricosene is C23H46. Its double bond joins C9 and C10, with the two chain segments on the same side.

prompt: In CH3CH=CHCH(CH3)CH(CH3)2, the two hydrogens on the double-bond carbons are on the same side of the double bond. What is the compound's name?

choices.text: cis-4,5-Dimethyl-2-hexene
trans-4,5-Dimethyl-2-hexene
choices.why: With both hydrogens on one side, the two alkyl groups are also on the same side, which is cis.

choices.text: cis-2,3-Dimethyl-4-hexene
choices.why: Number from the end nearer the double bond, so the double bond gets locant 2, not 4.

choices.text: cis-4,5-Dimethyl-3-hexene
choices.why: Counting from the CH3CH= end, the double bond runs from C2 to C3, so its locant is 2.

explanation: The six-carbon chain is numbered from the CH3CH= end, giving the double bond C2 and methyls on C4 and C5. The two alkyl groups on the double-bond carbons are on the same side, so the name is cis-4,5-dimethyl-2-hexene.

prompt: In (CH3)2CHCH2CH=CHCH2CH3, the two alkyl groups on the double-bond carbons are on opposite sides of the double bond. What is the compound's name?

choices.text: trans-6-Methyl-3-heptene
cis-6-Methyl-3-heptene
choices.why: Cis would mean the two alkyl groups are on the same side; here they are on opposite sides.

choices.text: trans-2-Methyl-4-heptene
choices.why: Number from the end nearer the double bond: from the CH3CH2 end it starts at C3, from the other end at C4.

choices.text: trans-6-Methyl-4-heptene
choices.why: Counting from the CH3CH2 end, which gives the methyl C6, the double bond starts at C3.

explanation: The seven-carbon chain is numbered from the CH3CH2 end, so the double bond starts at C3 and the methyl is on C6. With the two alkyl groups on opposite sides, the compound is trans-6-methyl-3-heptene.
